title: Why You Should Take Responsibility For Your Students' Behavior
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Marking his 700th article, Linsin reflects that the real value of his work, and of teaching itself, comes from taking responsibility rather than seeking credit. He argues that in an 'age of excuse,' it is easy and even defensible to attribute student misbehavior to home life, social media, or peer groups, but doing so surrenders a teacher's power to actually change outcomes. He illustrates this with a colleague who broke up a violent fight between two students, followed every protocol and consequence, yet turned inward afterward and asked only what she could have done better, rather than pointing outward. He argues that taking full responsibility regardless of outside forces is the single best thing a teacher can do to become happier and more effective, framing it as a kind of superpower that unlocks real influence over a class.
points: Real satisfaction in teaching comes from responsibility, not recognition or credit.
Attributing misbehavior to home life, social media, or peers is often true but forfeits a teacher's power to change it.
A colleague who broke up a violent student fight still asked only what she could improve, not why the students acted that way.
Taking 100 percent responsibility regardless of outside forces is the best path to becoming a happier, more effective teacher.
Ownership functions like a superpower, unlocking a teacher's ability to lead, influence, motivate, and control a class.
quotes: The satisfaction I get from writing about classroom management comes only through my responsibility to you.
We live in the age of excuse, of justification for every misstep, mistake, and failure.
But they’re still in your class. They still show up and sit in front of you every day. The question isn’t how they got that way.
My friend who broke up the fight was only concerned with what she could do better.
Her students were 100 percent responsible for their actions, yes. But she took 100 percent responsibility also.

Taking responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom—and your life for that matter—regardless of outside forces, is the best thing you can do to become a happier and more effective teacher.
You’re suddenly able to lead, influence, motivate, and control your class in ways you never thought possible.
